sections.body:
The nutrition panel is a small table of numbers printed on the back of a food pack. It exists because the law requires it. Every figure in it is given for a stated amount of the food, so that two products can be compared fairly.

It is worth knowing what it is not. It is not a menu, it is not a score, and it is not a verdict on whether the food is good for you. The same panel is printed on a bag of crisps and on a bag of lentils, and the numbers mean the same thing in both cases. Whether a food suits you depends on the rest of your diet, your health, and how much of it you eat.

The panel is built from three ideas.

A stated amount. Every number on the panel belongs to a serving. The panel says how big that serving is, in grams or millilitres, and sometimes also gives the figures for 100 g or 100 ml. The serving is chosen by the manufacturer, and it is often much smaller than what people actually eat. A cereal that claims 30 g a serving is describing a small bowl, not the one most people pour.

A reference amount. Alongside the figures there is a **reference intake** or **daily value**, which is a guide for an average adult per day. It is a yardstick, not a target. A person cycling forty kilometres a day does not need the same as a person at a desk, and a child needs less than an adult of the same weight. The daily value is a way of reading the numbers quickly: if sugar is more than a quarter of your daily value in one small portion, that is a fact worth knowing.

A set of nutrients. The panel lists energy, fat, saturates, carbohydrate, sugars, protein, salt or sodium, and often fibre. Some panels also list vitamins and minerals, and some list the amounts a single portion provides as a percentage of the daily reference.

Two numbers on the panel need converting before you use them. **Energy** is often given in kilocalories, and sometimes in kilojoules as well. One kilocalorie is 4.18 kilojoules. And **salt and sodium are not the same thing**: sodium is the element, salt is sodium chloride, and a label saying "salt" is telling you the total amount of both. Multiply sodium by 2.5 to get the salt it represents.

The panel is the numbers. The ingredient list on the same pack is the composition. You need both, and the panel is always the more precise of the two.
examples: The figures are for one serving, and the serving is 30 g, not the whole pack.
It says salt, so I do not need to work out the sodium separately.
One kilocalorie is 4.18 kilojoules, so both columns say the same thing.
sections.heading: What the nutrition panel is, and what it is not

sections.body:
Most people misread a nutrition panel because they read the serving size without checking it. This is the single most important habit on the back of a pack.

Look for the serving line first, and then ask the only question that matters: **is that what I eat?** A pack of crisps may list 30 g a serving, and a person may finish the whole 150 g bag in one go, which is five times the figures on the panel. A tub of yoghurt may say 170 g a serving, which is the whole tub. A bottle of juice may say 250 ml, which is the whole bottle, and the panel then reads like a warning when it is only describing the container.

If you eat a different amount, do the arithmetic. Multiply every figure by your multiplier. If your bowl is twice the stated serving, then double the energy, the sugar and the salt. This is rough, but it is far closer to the truth than reading the printed number as if it described your portion.

The **daily value** is the reference for an average adult. It lets you read the panel without doing any arithmetic at all. A food that gives you 30 % of the daily value of salt in one portion is a food that uses up a third of the day's allowance in one sitting. The percentages are printed on most panels and most people ignore them.

Where the reference amount is missing, use the per 100 g or per 100 ml line, which is the fair way to compare two products. It is also the line to use when you are comparing a fresh food with a packaged one, because a fresh food rarely has a serving at all.

And note the difference between **per serving** and **per portion**. They usually mean the same thing, and both are the manufacturer's choice. They are not the same as **per 100 g**, which is a regulatory standard that allows comparison. When two packs disagree, per 100 g is the honest number.

One trap worth naming: a product can be perfectly clear on the panel and still mislead you, because the manufacturer chose a small serving. If you compare two yoghurts by their front-of-pack calories per pot, you may be comparing a 100 g pot with a 170 g pot. Turn the pack over and compare per 100 g.
examples: The serving is 170 g and that is the whole tub, so I can read it straight off.
I eat about double the stated serving, so I double the sugar figure.
I compare the two packets per 100 g, because the pot sizes are different.
sections.heading: Serving sizes and the daily value

sections.body:
The three macronutrients are carbohydrate, fat and protein. They are the building materials of food and the energy the body runs on. Understanding what each one does makes the rest of the panel easy to interpret.

Carbohydrate is the body's main fuel. It breaks down into glucose, which goes into the blood and supplies energy, especially to the brain. The panel splits carbohydrate into **total carbohydrate**, which includes everything, and **sugars**, which are the carbohydrate that is a simple sugar. The difference between them is starch and fibre, which are digested more slowly and behave differently.

Starchy carbohydrates, such as rice, bread, potatoes and pasta, are the useful kind. They fill you up, they release energy over hours, and they usually come with fibre when they are minimally processed. Highly refined starch, such as white bread or white rice, is mostly carbohydrate with the fibre removed, which means it raises blood sugar quickly and does not fill you for long.

Fat is dense energy and the carrier of the vitamins A, D, E and K. The panel separates **total fat** into **saturates**, **polyunsaturates** and **monounsaturates**, and often gives a **trans fat** figure too. Saturates are the ones that matter most for heart health, and the guidelines consistently push them down and unsaturated fats up. Olive oil, nuts, seeds, oily fish and avocado are mostly unsaturated.

Protein is what your body is made of and what it repairs itself with. It is found in meat, fish, eggs, dairy, beans, lentils, soy and nuts. Most people in most countries get enough protein, and the panel figure is useful mainly for people restricting it deliberately.

Fibre, if it is listed, is the part of carbohydrate the gut cannot digest. It is in whole grains, vegetables, fruit, beans and nuts, and it is one of the few numbers on the panel where more is unambiguously better. It is the difference between feeling full after a meal and feeling hungry again an hour later.

A note on **energy**: one gram of fat carries about 9 kilocalories, one gram of carbohydrate or protein about 4, and one gram of alcohol about 7. This is why fat is so efficient, and why a food high in fat can carry more energy than a larger portion of something starchy.
examples: The carbs are mostly starch, and the sugars line is low, so I will have it.
It has 12 g of saturates, which is nearly a quarter of the daily value.
There is 6 g of fibre in this portion, which is a good amount for breakfast.
sections.heading: The macronutrients, and what each one does

sections.body:
Two groups of numbers carry most of the practical interest on a nutrition panel.

Sugars. The **total sugars** line includes every sugar in the product, both added and naturally present. **Sugars** also appear under another heading in some countries: **of which sugars**, which is the same total. Underneath, some panels separate **added sugars**, which is the part the manufacturer put in.

The distinction matters most for drinks and for anything aimed at children. A glass of orange juice has a lot of total sugar and no added sugar, because the sugar came with the fruit. A fizzy drink has total sugar and added sugar of about the same amount. A plain yoghurt has naturally occurring milk sugar and nothing added. A sweetened breakfast cereal can have a surprising amount of added sugar, often hidden under a different name in the ingredient list.

The free sugars that matter for health are the ones added, plus the ones in juice and dried fruit, because these do not come with fibre and do not fill you. A reasonable general target is around 30 g of free sugars a day for an adult, and a good deal less for a child.

Salt and sodium. Salt is sodium chloride. A label saying **salt** gives you the total amount, and a label saying **sodium** gives you the element alone. Divide sodium by 0.4 to get the salt it represents, or multiply salt by 0.4 to get the sodium. The general guidance is about 6 g of salt a day for an adult, which is a little under one teaspoon, and less for many people with high blood pressure. A large portion of packaged food can supply half of that on its own.

Read the salt line on the pack next to the serving size. A product with 1.2 g of salt per 100 g is not a high-salt product. A product with 1.2 g of salt per serving, in a portion you eat three times, is.

And check **saturates** while you are there. They are the fat that matters most for heart health, and the daily reference is around 20 g for an adult. Two thirds of that from a single snack is worth knowing.
examples: Total sugars are 22 g and added sugars are 18 g, so most of it is added.
This has 0.4 g of sodium per 100 g, so it is not a salty product.
One portion gives me 14 g of saturates, which is most of the daily guide.
sections.heading: Sugars, salt and the numbers most people want

sections.body:
The panel tells you how much. The ingredient list tells you what, and it is the better guide to what a product actually is.

Ingredients are listed by weight before the cooking, so the first ingredient is the heaviest thing in the pack. If the first three ingredients are flour, sugar and vegetable oil, that product is mostly those three, whatever the front of the pack says.

The list also reveals what the numbers cannot. Sugar hides under many names: sugar, glucose, fructose, sucrose, maltose, honey, syrup, concentrated fruit juice and maltodextrin. Two or three of those in one list means the product is much sweeter than the front suggests, and it also means that a product marketed as fruit-based may be mostly syrup.

Salt hides too, under salt, sodium, monosodium glutamate and the disodium forms used as raising agents. If you are cutting salt, look for the word sodium and not only the word salt.

The order also tells you about texture and processing. Flour first and sugar far down is a bread-like product. Sugar before flour is a cake, and it is reasonable to eat it as one.

Some ingredients carry a technical name you are not expected to know. Ascorbic acid is vitamin C. Niacin is vitamin B3. Tocopherol is vitamin E. Inulin is a type of fibre. You are not obliged to know them, but you are allowed to look them up, and a shop that cannot explain an ingredient has no business selling it to you.

Two more things the list tells you. **Allergens** are usually named in the list and sometimes repeated in a bold box: cereals containing gluten, crustaceans, eggs, fish, peanuts, soya beans, milk, nuts, celery, mustard, sesame, sulphur dioxide and sulphites above 10 mg/kg, lupin and molluscs. **Trace** means the ingredient is present in an amount too small to measure, usually under 0.5 %. **May contain** means the same production line was used, so the product can carry traces.

Read the list top to bottom once, and the panel once, and you know more about a product than its marketing does.
examples: Sugar appears twice under two names, so I know this is much sweeter than it looks.
I am looking for sodium rather than salt, because I am cutting both.
The allergen box says milk and soya, so this is not for my son.
sections.heading: The ingredient list, and what it adds that the numbers do not

sections.body:
These are the words you will meet on a pack and in a dietitian's advice, and what each one obliges the maker to do.

Per 100 g is the standard measure that lets you compare two products fairly. **Per serving** is whatever the maker calls a serving, which is convenient for them and unhelpful for you.

Reference intake is the daily average for an adult. **Daily value** is the American equivalent. The **percentage daily value** is the same figure expressed as a share of the day.

Kilocalorie (kcal) is a unit of energy in food. **Kilojoule (kJ)** is the same energy in the metric system, and one kilocalorie equals 4.18 kilojoules.

Sodium is the element that makes salt salty. **Salt** is sodium chloride, and a label quoting salt is quoting sodium plus the chloride that goes with it.

Saturates are the saturated fats, the part of the fat that matters most for blood cholesterol. **Added sugar** is sugar the manufacturer added, as distinct from sugar that arrived with the fruit or the milk.

Fibre is the part of carbohydrate the gut cannot digest. In some countries it is called dietary fibre or roughage, and the figure is sometimes called NSP, non-starch polysaccharide.

Claim means the front-of-pack statement, which is regulated but marketing-shaped. **Free from** means what is NOT in the product: no gluten, no added sugar, no dairy. It is only as good as the testing behind it.

Best served within and **once opened** are storage instructions. The second one means the clock starts when you open the pack, not when it was made.
sections.heading: The words on the panel, one by one

terms.example: One serving is 30 g, which is much less than the bowl I had.
terms.gloss: The amount of the food the nutrition figures are given for. It is the maker's choice, so it often does not match what you eat.

terms.example: One portion gives me 40 % of the daily value for salt.
terms.gloss: A daily guide for an average adult, used as the yardstick the percentages on a panel are measured against.

terms.example: The reference intake for energy is about 2000 kilocalories a day.
terms.gloss: The average daily amount of energy or a nutrient for an adult. A guide, not a target.

terms.example: The main macronutrient in this product is fat, not carbohydrate.
terms.gloss: One of the three nutrients the body needs in quantity: carbohydrate, fat and protein.

terms.example: It has 11 g of saturates, which is over half the daily reference.
terms.gloss: The saturated fats, which are the part of the fat that matters most for blood cholesterol.

terms.example: Total sugars are 20 g, and added sugars are 15 g of that.
terms.gloss: Sugar the manufacturer added, as distinct from sugar that came with the fruit or the milk.

terms.example: This has 0.5 g of sodium per 100 g, which is low.
terms.gloss: The element that makes salt salty. A label quoting salt is quoting sodium plus the chloride with it.

sections.body: The front of a pack is advertising, and it is regulated, but the shape of the words still does the work. "High in fibre" can mean 3 g per 100 g, which is modest in absolute terms. "No added sugar" says nothing about the sugar that came with concentrated fruit juice, and a product with no added sugar can contain more sugar than a cake. "Low fat" often means under 3 g of fat per 100 g, and a low-fat cake can be almost entirely sugar. "Source of protein" can mean three grams in a portion. "Natural" and "free from" describe what is absent or how something was made, not how good it is for you. "Lite" and "light" usually mean reduced energy, and sometimes mean reduced fat by a trivial amount. Read the front for what it claims, then turn the pack over and read the back for what it is.
sections.heading: Front-of-pack claims worth checking

sections.body:
Once you can read the panel, you can read it for a purpose. The rules of what to prioritise change with the question, and the same pack can be a good choice for one person and a poor one for another.

If you are managing diabetes or blood sugar. Look at **total sugars** and **carbohydrate**, and at where the carbohydrate comes from. Whole fruit, plain milk and unsweetened grains give a slower rise than fruit juice, white bread or sweetened cereal. Watch for **added sugar** on anything marketed as healthy. Carbohydrate counts matter too, because a portion with 40 g of carbohydrate is a different proposition from one with 15 g.

If you are managing high blood pressure. Look at **salt** or **sodium** first, and remember that a large part of it comes from processed food rather than the salt cellar. Then look at **saturates**. Ready meals, cured meat, salty snacks, stock cubes and sauces are the usual sources.

If you are trying to manage your weight. Use **energy** per 100 g, because it is the only comparison that is not distorted by pack size, and then look at **fibre** and **protein**, which tend to make a portion more filling. Energy density matters more than the word on the front. A food with 500 kilocalories per 100 g eaten in a portion of 30 g gives you 150 kilocalories; a food with 100 kilocalories per 100 g eaten in a portion of 300 g gives you 300.

If you have a food allergy or coeliac disease. Read the ingredient list and the allergen box, and read the manufacturing warning. If a product is not labelled with the allergen, do not assume it is safe. Ask the manufacturer rather than the shop assistant for anything you eat regularly.

If you are vegetarian or vegan. Read the ingredient list for the specific things you avoid, because some products contain animal-derived ingredients in small and unexpected places, and some are only vegetarian because of the flavouring.

If you have a medical condition that affects what you eat. Ask a dietitian, and take the packs with you. A printed panel cannot tell you whether a food is suitable for your particular diagnosis, and it is not a substitute for a plan built around your own results.
examples: For my blood pressure I look at salt first, and then the saturates.
This has 6 g of fibre per 100 g, which is worth having with breakfast.
I am comparing the two per 100 g, because the pack sizes are so different.
sections.heading: Reading a label for a specific need

sections.body: This is the routine that gets you most of the value in the shortest time. It works in a supermarket and it works in a small shop where the pack has been turned round.
examples: Serving is 25 g, I eat 50, so I double the sugar and the salt.
Per 100 g this one has 480 kilocalories and the other has 210.
Sugar is the second ingredient, so I am putting it back.
sections.heading: A sixty-second check at the shelf
steps: Turn the pack over and find the serving size.
Multiply the figures if you eat more or less than that serving.
Check the energy per 100 g against a product you already buy.
Look at sugars, and at added sugars if they are given.
Look at salt or sodium, and remember the sodium-to-salt conversion.
Read the first three ingredients, in order.
Check the allergen box if it matters to you.
Compare with the pack next to it, using the same unit both times.

sections.body:
Sometimes you need to ask, and it is worth knowing who to ask what.

The **shop assistant** knows the stock: which batch it is, how long it has been on the shelf, whether the shop makes its own bread or buys it in. Ask short, factual questions. "Is this the version with sugar in it?" is easier to answer accurately than "Is this healthy?". "Does this keep in the fridge once it is open?" and "Is there a smaller pack?" are both worth asking.

The **dietitian** is the professional who turns a number into a plan. A dietitian can work with your actual meals, your actual budget, your actual cooking time and your test results. Ask for the things that are specific: how much of this per week, how to read the label for the food I cook at home, and what to do on the days when I have no time. Bring the packs you eat most often.

The **doctor** can tell you which numbers matter for your particular condition and which do not. This matters more than it sounds, because advice about fat, salt, sugar and carbohydrates has changed over the years and varies between conditions. Ask what your test results are looking at, and what the specific threshold is that you are aiming for.

The manufacturer is the right place for anything about a single product: whether a claim is tested, whether a product really is free from gluten, what the serving is based on. Write, and keep the reply.

And ask the question that most people never ask: **is this a problem with my eating, or with this product?** Sometimes a person has spent a year avoiding a food because of a label they did not understand, and the honest answer is that the food was fine and the sleep was the problem.
examples: Does this one have sugar added, or just the sugar from the fruit?
Is there a smaller pack, or a single portion version?
Which of these numbers is the one my blood pressure results are looking at?
How much of this per week would you suggest, and how would I cook it?
sections.heading: Asking the shop, the dietitian and the doctor

item.summary: The nutrition panel is a set of numbers with a specific meaning, and the ingredient list is a set of names with a specific meaning. After reading this you can read any food label, judge a serving for yourself, compare two products fairly, check a claim on the front of the pack against the numbers behind it, and read a label with a specific medical need in mind.
item.title: Understanding Nutrition Facts and Food Ingredients
